catalog_locator: ch. 2 'Phonology' intro (p.20, PDF p.32) and sec. 2.3 'Stress' (pp.25-26, PDF pp.37-38); ch. 1 sec. 1.3 (c) 'Adaptation in word stress and intonation contours'…
catalog_quote: Stress is phonemic. ... 2.3 Stress. Stress is distinctive. Consider the following minimal pairs: ... Stress is a combination of pitch, force and length but pitch is the dominating element. Stress may occur on any syllable but the last syllable of words gets stress in a tiny minority of words only. No V.'V words have yet been found. Examples: ... 'V.CV head ... V.'CV mouth ... 'CV.CV.CV tongue ... CV.'CV.CV rain ... 'CV.CV bone ... CV.'CV palm wine ... V.CV.'CV star ... V.'CV.CV spear ... With some words stress has been found to vary, for example Imidol 'sand', Imidol 'sand'. ... [ch.1 (c) Adaptation in word stress and intonation contours:] Inanwatan has unpredictable, lexical word stress. Quite often the word stress of foreign words changes in borrowed words, e.g. regional Malay pandita>Inanwatan paditae '(male) minister'.

The author's earlier 2002 sketch (downloaded now to, pp.78, 81) states the same analysis. sources.quote: Word stress is unpredictable and distinctive (phonemic), cued mainly by pitch; minimal pairs given; a few words vary.
sources.locator: sec. 2 'Phonology', p.78 ('Stress is also phonemic (indicated phonemically with an acute accent on the vowel..)') and p.81 ('Word stress is unpredictable and distinctive. Stress is a combination of pitch, force and length but pitch is the dominating element; note the following pairs: awero above / awero grandmother, me?o rope / me?o wood, to?o bone / to?o palmwine. With some words stress has been found to vary, for example midol sand, midol sand.')
